results.title: Uber driver’s Find My iPhone app leads cops to accused carjacker, US cops say
results.body:
A man accused of stealing a 74-year-old Uber driver’s vehicle didn’t get far thanks to the victim’s Find My app, Michiganpolice say.

The Birmingham Police Department said the Uber driver was carjacked Thursday, March 30, by a man who “opened the driver’s door and began assaulting him.”

The suspect, whose identity was not publicly disclosed, pulled the driver out of his car and drove off, police said in a March 31 news release.

But the Uber driver, according to police, had a second phone that remained in the vehicle after it was stolen. Officers used the Find My app to track the car via that phone.

Officers found the vehicle about six miles away in Bloomfield Township. After a brief pursuit, the accused carjacker lost control of the car and struck a guardrail, according to police.

Police said the driver was taken into custody without incident. Charges were not announced.

The Find My app, originally known as Find My iPhone, enables a user to locate another missing Apple device.

Birmingham, Michigan is abut 20 miles northwest of Detroit. – The Charlotte Observer/Tribune News Service

It's not exactly clear how it is that you're the "legal owner" of a phone that has been assigned to a company's MDM. Did you buy this phone used?

That notwithstanding, if the phone was assigned to a company's MDM via their Apple Business Manager account (and not simply via User Approved enrollment), you will not be able to remove the MDM from the device without having the company release that device from their Apple Business Manager account, as well as the MDM server that the device was assigned to.

This is the whole point of "supervised" automated device enrollment (ADE, also previously known as DEP). If the company purchased the device for business use, nobody can claim that device as their own, without that company releasing the ABM/MDM lock on that device. The device reaches out to Apple's servers at boot time to see if it's owned by an Apple Business Manager account, and as such, it's inextricably locked to that company's ABM account.

Sorry to say that if your device is actually an ABM enrolled device, there's not much you can do besides contact the company that owns it and request that they release it from their ABM account and remove the MDM supervision/profiles from the device.

results.title: Apple issues warning to never put iPhone in rice for dangerous reaason – and what you should do instead - Internewscast
results.body:
Share this @internewscast.com

APPLE has warned that you must never place your iPhone in a bowl of rice.

Millions of people around the world are (wrongly) convinced that rice is the perfect way to dry out a wet iPhone.

But an Apple notice quietly published in 2022 confirms this as a myth.

The note reveals what to do if your iPhone gets wet and ends up with water in the Lightning port.

It lists three things you must never do, and placing it in rice is featured.

“Don’t put your iPhone in a bag of rice,” Apple warns.

“Doing so could allow small particles of rice to damage your iPhone.”

It’s very possible that these minute rice particles could make their way into your iPhone’s nooks and crannies.

They could get lodged in your charging port, or cause wear on your device.

And what’s worse: rice won’t do anything to dry your iPhone out faster.

Rice can’t absorb water from the air effectively enough to dry your iPhone out.

Maybe you’ve tried it in the past and it worked. The fact is that it would’ve worked even without the rice – and likely just benefitted from being left alone with the chance to dry.

So what should you really do when your iPhone is wet?

First look out for an iPhone notification that warns you if there’s water in your Lightning port.

That means you’re at risk of corrosion permanently damaging your phone.

Apple offers up three tips to dry out your iPhone.

“Tap your iPhone gently against your hand with the Lightning connector facing down to remove excess liquid,” Apple says.

“Leave your iPhone in a dry area with some airflow.”

After at least 30 minutes, Apple recommends trying to charge your phone again.

If you still see a water warning, you’ll need to leave your iPhone in a dry place with some airflow for up to a day.

Apple says it might take up to 24 hours for it to fully dry.

The iPhone maker recommends against drying it using an external heat source or compressed air.

You should also avoid inserting a foreign object like a cotton swap or paper towel into the Lightning connector.

results.title: People are getting into fights outside Apple stores because no one in China can buy an iPhone 6
results.body:
Fights have broken out all over the world in the last couple of days in front of Apple Stores as people queued for the new iPhone 6 and iPhone 6 Plus.

In part, the fights appear to be happening because Apple’s launch of the new phone is delayed in China, and Chinese immigrants are being paid to stand in line at Apple Stores in other countries to buy the new phones and sell them on to customers in China. The police believe the people lining up are all Chinese iPhone flippers:

“It’s our understanding that the markup on these phones when they’re resold in China can be upwards of 300 percent,” Hartman said in a phone interview. “For the most part, the dozens and hundreds of people who are waiting in line are just doing that.”

A black market iPhone 6 can go for $3,000 to $4,000, according to NBC. iPhone 6 has not launched in China due to a delay caused by Chinese officials, who have not yet approved the phone. China is one of the biggest markets for tech products — and not a single iPhone 6 is yet available there for sale, legally.

So black market resellers are organizing gangs of Chinese people to stand outside Western stores and buy as many iPhones as they can. Put together days-long lines, financially motivated customers, and a shortage of product, and the result is conflict.

Here’s a roundup of the trouble it’s causing.

A man was restrained by police in Paris after a scuffle broke out in front of an Apple store there. The Daily Mirror has this video of the man being handcuffed:

One man told The Mirror: “The store was very disorganised, they had not expected so many customers. Once the doors to the shopping centre was opened, people ran towards the shop and Apple staff had to call the police.”

Three people in New Haven, Conn., were arrested after a fight broke out between a dozen Chinese people who had driven up from New York to get iPhones, NBC says. New Haven police are not happy about it, according to Bloomberg:

“One has to ask the question to what degree is Apple responsible for contributing to this?” said Hartman of the New Haven Police Department. “You know we have a city to police, and this has been going on since Wednesday now.”

In Vancouver, Canada, police were called to control a line outside a shopping mall:

In New York, a fight briefly broke out in line for the store on the Upper West Side, according to USA Today. Twitter user Eli Blumenthal witnessed the fight:

Twitter / Eli Blumenthal

The fights illustrate the fact that the people who line up early for iPhone 6 are often not fans of the product. Rather, they’re people who are being paid to stand in line by resellers. As the Huffington Post noted when it inspected the lines in New York:

It was surprising that more than 90% of the people in line wearing warm jackets and sitting in portable chairs were Chinese. They weren’t Chinese tourists or Chinese-Americans, but the workers you often see doing the lowest-wage jobs in Chinatown.
